Theres a big problem with AI: even its creators cant explain how it works
That is not entirely true now is it

It is, but it doesn't necessarily mean what it seems like it would mean.

In 'traditional' programming if you wanted to write a program to, for instance, read english characters then you'd painstakingly try to formally describe each character in relation to one another. And in the end you'd spend hundreds of hours of work and your program would probably perform terribly and that's under optimal conditions. Get stylized or plain bad writing and the whole thing falls apart.

By contrast in a deep learning AI system instead of going from the big picture down to small you do the exact opposite. You create lots of little 'mini programs' that look are pieces of an input that in isolation would be irrelevant. So for instance if you scale the image of a character to be 10x10 you might have 100 little program pieces that each look at exactly one pixel. These in fire different values on different inputs - for instance a simple on/off depending on whether something was drawn in the part of the picture they're looking at. These outputs are then sent to a higher layer to starts to correlate their 'mini programs' outputs to a certain type of input. So for instance maybe on the character "X" mini programs 10-30 always fire while programs 50-80 never fire and the rest are kind of random. The upper level program would then be able to say if it's looking at an input with 10-30 on and 50-80 off that it's probably looking at an X so long as no other character ended up with an even stronger correlation. This process can be multiple layers deep and thousands of 'mini programs' deep all making the correlations stronger and stronger. And of course the little mini programs can do anything. Maybe one fires if there is a width of at least 3 horizontal blocks set in the input image. It's a lot of words to describe but it's actually a pretty simple process at the most fundamental level - and unbelievably effective.

So anyhow, the long and short of this is that the actual programmer will be unable to explain in any meaningful way why the program might, for instance, see an "X" as a "Y" other than the training created faulty correlations given the set of 'mini programs' he setup. This is why, for instance, creating deep learning systems to kill or destroy is a really really bad idea for now. We can obviously create fail safes, but we will never be able to predict all potential forms of aberrant behavior. All you can do is train it as well as you can and then hope that future behavior will behave in accordance with past training. Alot like a human I suppose.
